title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Timber floor restoration
audience: Owners of small Australian property trade businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short jobs, and explain it to a client before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A timber floor rate depends on your skill with sanding, edging and finishing, the equipment you own, how well you handle dust control and old finishes, and the cost of running the business. A restorer who can refinish, repair small boards and recoat in one visit may justify a higher rate than one who only buffs. Do not cut the rate to win work. The Oneflare guide's general refinish range of $25 to $50 per square metre is a sourced area range, with no date and no location, so use it only as a sense check (Oneflare, no date shown). Its state table is not used as a rate because the unit is unclear.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every hour of the week can be billed. Few can. Travel between jobs, quoting, admin, marketing, sander and extractor upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid working hours in a year, subtract the non-billable time, and you have billable hours. Jobber's guide puts billable time at about 60 to 80 percent of working hours, a general range rather than an Australian figure (Jobber, 5 November 2024, modified 20 July 2026). Floor work often means long days of sanding with setup and clean-down between rooms, so log one month before you rely on the range.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, registration, equipment and its upkeep, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income you need. A business.gov.au pricing guide says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure, so decide how each applies to you (business.gov.au, 1 October 2026). Have a registered tax agent confirm how leave and superannuation are treated in your situation before the rate is published. Divide the total by billable hours to reach the base rate. A personal-training guide from AIPT works backwards from a target income, dividing by working weeks and then by weekly hours, with tax and business costs added on top (AIPT, 16 May 2025). Review the base rate each quarter.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short jobs
instruction.body: A small hallway or a single-board repair can cost more in time than it earns, because travel, protection, dust control and clean-down do not shrink with the job. A minimum charge covers the time to attend the site and start work. Contractor+ suggests setting a minimum from the full cost of the visit, divided by one minus the target margin, with the minimum covering travel, set-up and clean-up. Its figures are labelled illustrative and are not used here (Contractor+, 23 September 2026). Set the minimum from your own visit cost, state it before the booking, and explain it in plain terms.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, marketing, training, equipment upkeep and leave to find billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, equipment, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up, dust control and admin for a short job, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: A restorer's calculation shows that only sixty of every hundred paid hours can be billed, but the owner plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate if the wrong assumption is kept?
workedExamples.reasoning: Pricing as if every paid hour were billable understates the rate, because the costs and the income still have to come out of the hours that can be billed. With sixty billable hours in every hundred, the costs of all one hundred paid hours must come from the sixty, so the rate needs to be about 1.67 times the rate for a fully billable week. The rate is built from billable hours, then checked against the area range as a sense check and against the minimum charge before it is published.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative: a restorer is asked to fix two loose boards in a small 4 square metre hallway. The visit takes 1.5 hours on site, with 30 minutes of travel and 30 minutes of protection and clean-down.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the hourly rate alone price this visit?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The hourly rate, applied to the 1.5 hours on site, leaves the travel, protection and clean-down unpaid, so the effective rate is lower than the quoted one. A minimum charge that covers travel, set-up, dust control and admin is the better answer, and it is stated before the booking.

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a published average or a competitor's figure without checking your own costs. Gap: no sourced timber rate with a date and location exists.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with your quotes and the local evidence you can verify.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking short jobs at the same rate, without covering travel, protection and clean-down.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law, as summarised in the ACCC price display guidance (2 October 2026). That guidance says the total must include unavoidable fees. It does not settle whether a minimum or call-out charge is a fair term. Check that point with current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.
Confirm how leave, superannuation and tax apply to your business with a registered tax agent. This lesson gives no tax advice.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short job.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against your own quotes and verified local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short jobs. Gap: no sourced timber minimum charge exists.

knowledgeChecks.question: A restorer can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average on a vendor's website and the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for a short floor repair?
options: Because a short job needs travel but no set-up or clean-down at all
Because travel, protection and clean-down time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate for timber floor work?
options: A single published national average from another trade
Your own costs and billable hours, compared with verifiable local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The first price shown on a bidding site this week

officialReferences.title: Price displays (ACCC)
officialReferences.covers: States that the total price must include unavoidable fees, shown as a single figure. Does not address minimum or call-out charges, or tax on leave and superannuation, which remain unconfirmed. Publisher: ACCC.
